source.title: Time Matters: Scaling Laws for Any Budget

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling-law loss prediction on new transformer configurations and evaluates a hyperparameter-based prediction method; it is a conceptual test rather than an explicit replication of either original study.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on fitted and predicted loss, including comparisons of fitted coefficients. It also reports runtime-prediction results (r2 = 0.74) and a memory-copy ablation, but these measure throughput rather than the loss-scaling versions and are not included as rows. It proposes architectural choices from predicted loss gradients, but does not report a controlled measured-loss comparison at fixed parameter count and fixed token count.
record.test_reason: It fits the Chinchilla loss form with Hoffmann et al.'s exponents to 1,535 small C4 decoder-only transformers (319K–310M parameters) trained for a fixed 3 hours. It reports the fit quality and shows that the published coefficients fail on its data. This is a new small-scale, fixed-wall-clock setting with results bearing on V1 and V7. Most of the paper is its own runtime-based loss predictor, which is method performance, not a test of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct; additions are needed. The authors conclude that final loss can be predicted from hyperparameters alone by combining a Chinchilla-form law with a memory-copy runtime estimate, and that memory copies beat FLOPs as a runtime predictor. They report that published Chinchilla coefficients underestimate loss by over 2x on their data, which they read as setup-sensitivity of the coefficients while 'the exponents are more robust'. The wider/shallower recommendation is a prediction from their equation, not a measured result. They note that sharding and scale beyond a few hundred million parameters are not considered.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a Chinchilla-style loss law but fits its own linear coefficients and combines the law with a memory-copy-based runtime estimate to predict loss from hyperparameters.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted loss coefficients depend on which published coefficient set is used: the paper's own coefficients differ from those of Hoffmann et al. and Besiroglu et al. on the same data.

fits_no_version.finding: Memory copies predict per-step runtime better than FLOPs (overall r2 0.74). The fit is tighter for larger models, and the memcpy term carries almost all the explanatory power.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FLOP-based compute is a poor proxy for wall-clock cost, so compute-based scaling laws mis-specify cost for small models.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a fixed wall-clock budget, the fitted law predicts that wider and shallower models reach lower loss at constant parameter count (Figure 6). This is a model prediction only; loss was not measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With a fixed training time, the best architecture shape is set by throughput, favouring wide, shallow models.

record.problems: The experiments are limited to decoder-only transformers trained on C4, with models up to a few hundred million parameters for the loss experiments; the authors also state that they do not consider model sharding or scale beyond a few hundred million parameters. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Runtime-prediction and memory-copy/FLOPs ablation results in Sections 5 and Figure 3 were left out because they measure runtime prediction rather than any listed loss-scaling claim version. The architecture-gradient prediction in Figure 6 was not recorded as a result row because it is not a controlled measured-loss comparison at fixed parameter count and token count.

untested.parts: The exponents are not independently estimated (they are fixed to Hoffmann's). The models span only about 3 orders of magnitude in parameters, all small. No single-variable power law is tested with the other variables non-limiting.
There is no prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs. The holdout is within the same size range.
Compute-optimal N and D are not fitted across budgets.
V4 is assumed as the 'Parameter Equivalence Heuristic', not tested. Figure 6 gives predicted gradients under a fixed time budget, not measured loss at fixed N and D.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
The exponents are never refit, so it is untested whether they depend on setup. Curvature away from a power law is not examined.

missing.what: Figure 5 compares the Chinchilla fit using empirical versus estimated data consumption. The text says r2 matches (0.9) and that there is essentially no added error.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V2 label is removed: the holdout is not larger than the fitting runs, and R6 is the study's own method. The study assumes V4 (Principle 1) rather than testing it. The authors' remark that exponents are robust rests on linear rescaling of predictions that use fixed Hoffmann exponents. No alternative exponents were tried, so it is not evidence against V7's exponent clause. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The study is a short preprint, models are at most 310M parameters, and the vocabulary is fixed at 8,000.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests a Chinchilla-form loss fit on its C4 transformer configurations, not the full range of language models, training regimes, or several orders of magnitude specified by the claim.
The held-out configurations are within the reported model-size range; the study does not test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs.
It does not fit parameter-count and token-count optima across compute budgets or test whether either grows as a power of compute.

It does not isolate architecture effects on measured loss while holding both parameter count and training tokens fixed. Its architecture-gradient result is a prediction from its model, not such a controlled comparison.
No other modalities, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer setting is tested.

The study compares loss-fit coefficients and reports their setup sensitivity, but does not test whether exponents or compute-optimal allocations change, or whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.note: Aggregate result for the fitting configurations; loss was fitted using Hoffmann et al.'s exponents and the paper's own A, B, and E coefficients.
rows.check: Link is fine. Exponents were fixed to Hoffmann et al.'s values, not fitted, so only the linear coefficients A, B, E come from this data. Tokens vary with model speed under a fixed 3-hour budget, not independently. Text says the fit is evaluated on a 767-config holdout.

rows.subject: 767 held-out decoder-only transformer model configurations (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Predict final loss from model hyperparameters using the tuned loss law and estimated training speed, then compare with actual loss.

conditions.value: 3 hours; single TPU, no model sharding

rows.measure: fit between predicted and actual final loss
rows.note: Aggregate holdout result. The authors compare it with r2 = 0.9 for the traditional Chinchilla fit; the holdout is not orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs.
rows.check: This is the study's own method: loss predicted from hyperparameters via a runtime estimator, r2 0.92. The holdout sits in the same 319K–310M range as the fitting runs, so it says nothing about extrapolation to much larger runs (V2). The row should be relabelled as method performance.

relationships.condition: Decoder-only transformers, 319K–310M parameters, C4, 3-hour runs, Hoffmann exponents fixed and A/B/E fitted
relationships.reason: The Chinchilla form gives r2 = 0.9 on holdout configurations (R1, R5). The support is weak because the exponents were imposed, not fitted.
relationships.display_finding: The Chinchilla-form fit achieved R² of 0.9 on held-out configurations, with scaling exponents fixed rather than estimated.

relationships.condition: Published Chinchilla coefficient sets applied to this study's small C4 models
relationships.reason: Hoffmann and Besiroglu coefficients give fitted slopes 0.43–0.48 and intercepts 1.50–1.70, versus 1.00/0.00 for local coefficients. The authors call the coefficients 'highly sensitive to the details of the setup' (R2–R4).
relationships.display_finding: Published coefficients yield fitted slopes of 0.43–0.48 and intercepts of 1.50–1.70, versus a slope of 1.00 and intercept of 0.00 for locally fitted coefficients.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
